name: Paul

seo.title: Saint Paul the Apostle: his life, his letters and how he died
seo.description: Paul in plain words: the persecutor stopped on the road to Damascus, his journeys, shipwrecks and letters, his death in Rome, and the myths.

band.where: Tarsus, the Roman East and Rome
band.lede: He hunted the first Christians until a light stopped him on the road to Damascus. Then he carried the faith across the Roman world.

picture.alt: A painting: Paul, balding, with a long red-brown beard, sits at a wooden table writing with a quill, his eyes on the page. He wears a dark green tunic and a bright red cloak. Open books, loose sheets and a scroll lie on the table, and the hilt of a sword stands at the right edge.
picture.credit: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, attributed to Valentin de Boulogne, about 1618 to 1620. Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. Public domain.
picture.creator: Valentin de Boulogne

card.line: The persecutor who became the apostle to the Gentiles. His name is on nearly half the books of the New Testament.

filters.alias: saul saul of tarsus apostle paulus pablo paolo pavel pawel tentmaker damascus letters epistles gentiles

who: Paul, first called Saul, was a Jew from Tarsus, a Pharisee and a Roman citizen. He hunted the first Christians until the risen Jesus stopped him on the road to Damascus. Then he became the apostle to the Gentiles, and took the faith across the Roman world. He died a martyr at Rome under Nero.

roles.name: Pharisee
roles.line: Taught at the feet of Gamaliel

roles.name: Apostle
roles.line: Called on the road to Damascus

lines: Five times, by his own count
Once he spent a night and a day in the open sea
More than 40 men had sworn to kill him

numbers.chip: On board the ship that ran aground

lines: Nearly half the books of the New Testament
Seven are accepted as his by nearly all scholars

tidbits.text: The saying about scales falling from someone's eyes comes from his story. As Ananias laid his hands on him in Damascus, “something like scales fell from Saul's eyes”.
He quotes words of Jesus that are in none of the four Gospels: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
He quoted Greek poets. Jerome names three: Epimenides on the Cretans, Menander for “Bad company corrupts good character”, and Aratus for “We are His offspring”.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: At **Tarsus** in Cilicia, in today's Turkey, “a citizen of no ordinary city”. No one recorded the year. Jerome says the family came to Tarsus from Gischala, in the Holy Land.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Of the **tribe of Benjamin**, “a Hebrew of Hebrews”. A Pharisee, “the son of a Pharisee”. A **Roman citizen** from birth. His sister's son lived in Jerusalem.

facts.label: Married?
facts.text: **Unmarried** when he wrote 1 Corinthians: “It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am.” Clement of Alexandria thought he had a wife, and left her at home for the work.

facts.label: Schooling
facts.text: In Jerusalem, “at the feet of Gamaliel”, a teacher of the law honoured by all the people.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **tentmaker**, like his friends Priscilla and Aquila. He paid his own way: “these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs”.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Saul**, his Hebrew name, the name of Israel's first king, who was also of the tribe of Benjamin. **Paul**, his Roman name. **The apostle to the Gentiles**, his own words.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: At **Rome**, under the emperor **Nero**, in the 60s. The early writers say he was **beheaded**. Jerome puts it on the same day as Peter's death.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: By the **road to Ostia**, says Jerome. The basilica of **St Paul Outside the Walls** marks the grave.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: **Thirteen letters** of the New Testament open with his name. Who wrote six of them is debated. **Hebrews**, which names no author, was long counted his too. See His letters, below.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: **Missionaries**, **evangelists**, **writers**, **journalists** and **publishers**, in the Catholic Church, says *Britannica*.

portrait.alt: A painting by Rubens: Paul, an old man with thick grey-brown curls and a long full beard, glances to the left. He wears a deep blue cloak over a dark robe. One hand grips a sword by its carved hilt, and the other rests on a closed book.
portrait.credit: Saint Paul, Peter Paul Rubens, about 1611. Museo del Prado, Madrid. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A painting by Peter Paul Rubens, about 1611. It belongs to a set of the apostles he painted for the Duke of Lerma. He holds a sword, his sign in art. Museo del Prado, Madrid. Public domain.

typeNote: The Forge is serious by nature, and at its best with something to do. The test sets Paul against Barnabas, the Hearth, over young Mark: Barnabas gave him a second chance, and Paul would not. Years later Paul wrote, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.”

west.text: The **Conversion of Paul**, a **Catholic** feast. A Festival in the **Church of England**, and kept by the **Episcopal Church** and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**. It closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.
**Peter and Paul**, a **Catholic** solemnity. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.
The **Commemoration of Paul**, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology** and the 1962 Missal. Since 1969 Rome keeps the day for the first martyrs of Rome.
The **dedication of the basilicas** of Peter and Paul in Rome. A **Catholic** optional memorial.

east.text: **Peter and Paul**, the leaders of the apostles, for the **OCA** and the **Greek** churches.
All **twelve apostles** together, the next day, in the **OCA**.
The **Coptic** Church, on 5 Abib in its own calendar: the martyrdom of Peter and Paul. The **Russian Church**'s 29 June falls on this day too.

feasts.note: Why a day of his own on 30 June? The *Catholic Encyclopedia* explains. On 29 June the pope went from St Peter's to St Paul's, about five miles apart, and the double ceremony was too tiring. So Paul's part moved to the next day. Rome's calendar of 1969 notes that the *Martyrology of Jerome* already marks his conversion on 25 January. Books from Gaul keep it as a feast by the end of the 700s. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later.

said.lede: Jesus, his friends, his critics and the first generations after him, in their own words.

quotes.q: This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.
quotes.who: Jesus, to Ananias, who was afraid to go to him

quotes.q: The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.
quotes.who: The churches of Judea, which had never seen his face, as he tells it

quotes.q: His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.
quotes.who: His critics at Corinth, as he quotes them

quotes.q: Consider also that our Lord's patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him.
quotes.who: The second letter under Peter's name

quotes.q: For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul.
quotes.who: Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to the church at Philippi, which Paul had founded

cite.text: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 3

quotes.q: Paul's heart was His heart, and a tablet of the Holy Spirit, and a book of grace.
quotes.who: John Chrysostom, preaching on Romans, about the man who wrote, “Christ lives in me”

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans, Homily 32

moments.title: Stephen's death
moments.text: Stephen, the first martyr, was dragged out of the city and stoned. “Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.” Stephen fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Acts adds, “And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen's death.” Then Saul began to destroy the church. He went from house to house and dragged off men and women to prison.

moments.title: A light from heaven
moments.text: Saul asked the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so he could bring the Lord's followers back to Jerusalem in chains. Near the city a light flashed around him, “brighter than the sun”. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” “Who are You, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, Whom you are persecuting.” The men with him heard the voice but saw no one. Saul got up blind, and they led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days he did not eat or drink.

moments.title: “Brother Saul”
moments.text: The Lord sent a disciple named Ananias to him. Ananias was afraid. “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem.” He went anyway, and placed his hands on the man. “Brother Saul,” he said. At once Saul could see again. He was baptised, and began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. All who heard him were astounded. “Isn't this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name?”

moments.title: Over the wall in a basket
moments.text: He went away into Arabia, he writes, and came back to Damascus. Then some of the Jews plotted to kill him. Day and night they watched the city gates. So one night his disciples lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall. Paul tells it himself, in a list of things he could boast of. The governor under King Aretas was guarding the city to arrest him, “But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp.”

moments.title: Barnabas speaks for him
moments.text: In Jerusalem he tried to join the disciples, “but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.” Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles, and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road. Paul says he stayed fifteen days with Cephas, that is Peter. When some of the Greek-speaking Jews tried to kill him, the believers took him down to Caesarea and sent him home to Tarsus.

moments.title: Where they were first called Christians
moments.text: Years later, Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and brought him back to Antioch. For a full year the two of them taught large numbers of people there. “The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.” When a prophet foretold a famine, the church sent help to the believers in Judea, carried by Barnabas and Saul.

moments.title: “Saul, who was also called Paul”
moments.text: The church at Antioch was worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” They sailed to Cyprus, with John Mark as their helper. At Paphos the Roman governor, Sergius Paulus, sent for them to hear the word of God. From that day on, Acts calls him Paul. On the mainland, at Perga, Mark left them and went home to Jerusalem.

moments.title: Zeus, Hermes, and then stones
moments.text: When Paul healed a man lame from birth, the crowd shouted, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, “because he was the chief speaker.” The priest of Zeus brought bulls and wreaths to offer them a sacrifice. The two tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd: “We too are only men, human like you.” Then Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over. They stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead. The disciples gathered around him. He got up and went back into the city.

moments.title: A sharp disagreement
moments.text: Paul wanted to go back and visit the churches they had founded. Barnabas wanted to take John Mark. Paul thought it best not to, because Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia. “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus. Paul chose Silas and set out by land. John Chrysostom saw two gifts at work. One was “more tender and indulgent, but this one more strict and austere,” and he saw God's plan in the parting.

cite.text: Acts 15:36-41; John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts, Homily 34

moments.title: Singing in the stocks
moments.text: In a night vision a man of Macedonia begged him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” So Paul crossed into Europe. At Philippi he freed a slave girl from a spirit, and her owners dragged him and Silas before the magistrates. They were beaten with rods and put in the stocks. “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God.” An earthquake shook the prison, and every door flew open. The jailer was about to kill himself when Paul called out, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” In the morning Paul refused to slip away quietly. They were Roman citizens, beaten without a trial: “Let them come themselves and escort us out!”

moments.title: To an unknown god
moments.text: Paul was deeply disturbed to see Athens full of idols. He argued in the marketplace every day. Some philosophers asked, “What is this babbler trying to say?” At the Areopagus he began, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.” He had found an altar inscribed TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. “Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.” He quoted their own poets. When he spoke of the resurrection of the dead, some began to mock. Others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” A few believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.

moments.title: Tentmakers
moments.text: At Corinth he met Aquila and his wife Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius. “They were tentmakers by trade, just as he was”, so he stayed and worked with them. One night the Lord spoke to him in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent. For I am with you.” He stayed a year and a half, teaching the word of God.

moments.title: The riot of the silversmiths
moments.text: At Ephesus, people who had practised magic burned their books in public. The books were worth fifty thousand drachmas. Then a silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, warned his fellow craftsmen that Paul was ruining their trade. “He says that man-made gods are no gods at all.” The whole city rushed into the theatre. Paul wanted to go in, but the disciples would not let him. For about two hours the crowd shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Most of them did not even know why they were there. At last the city clerk calmed them and sent them home.

moments.title: The last goodbye
moments.text: Paul sent for the elders of the church at Ephesus. He told them the Holy Spirit warned him in town after town that chains awaited him. “But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course.” He reminded them that he had worked with his own hands to help the weak. Then he knelt down with them all and prayed. “They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him.” What grieved them most was that they would never see his face again.

moments.title: Arrested
moments.text: Jews from Asia saw him in the temple and stirred up the crowd. They dragged him out and were trying to kill him when Roman soldiers ran down. The commander had him bound with two chains. As they stretched him out to be flogged, Paul asked, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?” The commander said he had paid a high price for his own citizenship. “But I was born a citizen,” Paul replied. Then more than forty men swore not to eat or drink until they had killed him. The son of Paul's sister heard of the plot and warned him. That night the Romans sent him to the governor at Caesarea, under a heavy guard.

moments.title: “I appeal to Caesar!”
moments.text: The governor Felix kept him in prison for two years, hoping for a bribe. When Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix grew frightened. The next governor, Festus, asked if he would stand trial in Jerusalem. Paul refused: “I appeal to Caesar!” Before King Agrippa he told his story again. Festus shouted, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” Agrippa asked, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” “Short time or long,” Paul replied, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.”

moments.place: The sea off Crete, then Malta
moments.title: Shipwreck
moments.text: Paul warned that sailing on had become dangerous. No one listened. A wind called the Northeaster caught the ship, and for many days neither sun nor stars appeared. Paul stood up among the men. An angel had told him, “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar.” On the fourteenth night he urged them all to eat. He took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, and broke it. At daybreak the ship struck a sandbar and broke up. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, but the centurion stopped them to save Paul. “In this way everyone was brought safely to land.”

moments.title: Boldly and freely
moments.text: Believers walked out along the road to meet him, and when Paul saw them he took courage. In Rome he was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. “Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him.” Acts ends there, with Paul still waiting for his trial. Its last verse says of him: “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.”

miracles.lede: Acts says “God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul”. Paul himself said where the power came from:

pledge.q: I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in leading the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God.

items.title: The man who had never walked
items.text: A man in Lystra had been lame from birth and had never walked. He was listening to Paul. Paul looked straight at him, and saw that he had faith to be healed. In a loud voice he called out:
items.witness: The man jumped up and began to walk. The crowd took Paul and Barnabas for gods.

items.title: Handkerchiefs and aprons
items.text: Even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were carried to the sick,
items.quote: and the diseases and evil spirits left them

items.title: Eutychus
items.text: Paul talked on until midnight in an upper room full of lamps. A young man named Eutychus sat in the window, sinking into a deep sleep. He fell from the third story and was picked up dead. Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and put his arms around him.
items.quote: Do not be alarmed! He is still alive!
items.witness: Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and talked on until daybreak. The people took the boy home alive, greatly relieved.

items.title: Publius's father
items.text: Publius, the chief official of Malta, took the shipwrecked men in for three days. His father was sick in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, prayed, placed his hands on him, and healed him. After that,
items.quote: the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well

more.title: The sorcerer struck blind
more.text: On Cyprus, a sorcerer named Elymas tried to turn the governor from the faith. Paul looked straight at him and spoke. Mist and darkness came over Elymas, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand, as Paul had once been led. The governor believed.
more.quote: Now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.

more.title: The fortune-teller
more.text: At Philippi a slave girl with a spirit of divination earned her owners a large income. For many days she followed Paul, shouting after him. At last he grew so annoyed that he turned and spoke to the spirit, and it left her that very moment.
more.quote: In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!

more.title: The seven sons of Sceva
more.text: At Ephesus, travelling exorcists tried to use the name Paul preached: “I command you by Jesus, Whom Paul proclaims.” Seven sons of a chief priest named Sceva were doing it. The man with the evil spirit leapt on them, and they ran out of the house naked and wounded. The spirit had answered them first:
more.quote: Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?

more.title: The viper
more.text: On Malta, Paul laid a bundle of sticks on the fire, and a viper fastened itself to his hand. The islanders decided he must be a murderer. He shook it off into the fire and suffered no harm. They waited for him to swell up or drop dead. When nothing happened,
more.quote: they changed their minds and said he was a god

words.note: Thirteen letters in the New Testament bear his name, and Acts records his speeches. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.q: Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
feature.ctx: He wrote it to the church at Corinth, which was split into factions and proud of its spiritual gifts.

quotes.q: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
quotes.who: From his letter to the Romans.

quotes.q: I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, Who loved me and gave Himself up for me.
quotes.who: From his letter to the Galatians.

quotes.q: For I am the least of the apostles and am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain.
quotes.who: Looking back, in his first letter to Corinth.

quotes.q: That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
quotes.who: He had begged the Lord three times to take away “a thorn in my flesh”. The answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you.”

quotes.q: For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
quotes.who: From prison, in chains, to the church at Philippi.

quotes.q: I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. In any and every situation I have learned the secret of being filled and being hungry, of having plenty and having need. I can do all things through Christ Who gives me strength.
quotes.who: Thanking the Philippians for a gift they sent him in prison.

extras.title: His letters
extras.lede: Thirteen letters of the New Testament open with Paul's name. Christians have always read them as Scripture. Who wrote six of them is debated today, and so is Hebrews, which names no author. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: To churches and to friends
items.text: Jerome counts “nine epistles to seven churches”: Rome, Corinth, Galatia, Ephesus, Philippi, Colossae and Thessalonica. Four more go to friends: two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon. Paul did not always hold the pen. In Romans the scribe, Tertius, adds his own greeting. Paul often wrote the last lines himself:
items.quote: This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write.

cite.text: 2 Thessalonians 3:17; Romans 16:22; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 5

items.title: The seven
items.text: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Nearly all scholars accept these seven as his. *Britannica* calls them the seven “accepted as being entirely authentic”.

items.title: The six in doubt: the case against
items.text: Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus. Many modern scholars think these came from followers writing in Paul's name, as *Britannica* puts it. They point to differences in the words, the style, and the way the churches are run. Of the letters to Timothy and Titus, the Scottish scholar James Moffatt wrote in the *Encyclopaedia Biblica*:
items.quote: Favourite Pauline phrases and words are totally wanting.

cite.text: James Moffatt, in the Encyclopaedia Biblica, volume 4, as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia, “Pastoral Epistles”; Britannica

items.title: The six in doubt: the case for
items.text: The early Church received all thirteen as his. About 180, Irenaeus wrote of Rome's second bishop: “Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy.” Those who hold that Paul wrote all thirteen say his other letters differ from one another too, and that his scribes, his readers and the years between explain the rest. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* answered Moffatt:
items.quote: the early and universal tradition ascribing the whole of them to the Apostle is correct.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Pastoral Epistles”

items.title: And Hebrews?
items.text: Hebrews names no author. Eusebius counted “Paul's fourteen epistles”, but noted that the church of Rome disputed Hebrews. Jerome says it was not counted his because of its style and language. Tertullian thought Barnabas wrote it, and others named Luke, or Clement of Rome. Origen's verdict, which Eusebius kept:
items.quote: But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 3, and Book 6, chapter 25; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 5

myths.claim: He fell off his horse on the road to Damascus.
myths.truth: Acts never mentions a horse. “He fell to the ground,” says Acts. Paul told King Agrippa, “We all fell to the ground.” The horse comes from painters, Caravaggio among them. Acts puts Paul on a mount just once, years later, as a prisoner: the Romans brought “mounts for Paul” to carry him to the governor by night.

cite.text: Acts 9:4; 26:14; 23:23-24; Caravaggio, The Conversion of Saint Paul, 1601

myths.claim: Saul changed his name to Paul when he became a Christian.
myths.truth: Acts goes on calling him Saul for years. Ananias greets him as “Brother Saul”, and the Holy Spirit says, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul.” The change comes later, on Cyprus, in a single line: “Saul, who was also called Paul”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says Jews of his day often had two names, one Hebrew and one Latin or Greek. As a Roman citizen he had a Latin one. Jerome thought he took it from Sergius Paulus, the governor of Cyprus, his first convert there. Augustine heard humility in it, since {la|paulus} means small.

cite.text: Acts 9:17; 13:2, 9; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Paul”; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 5; Augustine, a sermon for 29 June, given by the OCA

myths.claim: We know what Paul looked like: short, bald and bow-legged.
myths.truth: The Bible never describes his face. The famous picture comes from the *Acts of Paul and Thecla*, a story written in the second century. It sees him as “a man little of stature, thin-haired upon the head, crooked in the legs, of good state of body, with eyebrows joining, and nose somewhat hooked, full of grace”. Tertullian says the presbyter in Asia who wrote it was found out. He confessed “that he had done it from love of Paul”, and lost his office.

cite.text: Acts of Paul, tr. M. R. James (1924); Tertullian, On Baptism, chapter 17

myths.claim: Paul was one of the Twelve.
myths.truth: He was not. After Judas died, “the lot fell to Matthias.” Paul was called later, on the road, and he claimed the name apostle all the same: “Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” Jerome calls him “an apostle outside the number of the twelve apostles”.

cite.text: Acts 1:26; 1 Corinthians 9:1; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 5

circle.name: Barnabas
circle.text: The “Son of Encouragement”. He brought Saul to the apostles when they were all afraid of him, fetched him from Tarsus to Antioch, and travelled with him to Cyprus and Lystra. They parted over Mark. Later Paul wrote of him as a fellow apostle who, like Paul, worked for a living.

circle.name: Peter
circle.text: Paul stayed fifteen days with him in Jerusalem. Later, at Antioch, Peter drew back from eating with Gentile believers, and Paul writes, “I opposed him to his face.” The second letter under Peter's name calls him “our beloved brother Paul”. The early writers say both died at Rome under Nero.

cite.text: Galatians 1:18; 2:11; 2 Peter 3:15; Eusebius, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25

circle.name: Mark
circle.text: John Mark, Barnabas's cousin. He left Paul and Barnabas at Perga and went home, and Paul would not take him again. Years later Mark was at Paul's side while Paul was a prisoner, and at the end Paul asked for him.

circle.name: Timothy
circle.text: A young disciple from Lystra, with a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father. Paul called him “my true child in the faith”, and told the Philippians, “I have nobody else like him.”

circle.name: Luke
circle.text: “Luke, the beloved physician”. At Troas the story in Acts turns from “they” to “we”. Irenaeus took that as proof “that this Luke was inseparable from Paul”. Near the end Paul wrote, “Only Luke is with me.”

cite.text: Colossians 4:14; Acts 16:10; 2 Timothy 4:11; Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 14

circle.name: Silas
circle.text: A leader of the Jerusalem church, whom Paul chose after he parted from Barnabas. He was beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi, and sang hymns with him at midnight. The letters call him Silvanus.

circle.name: Priscilla and Aquila
circle.text: A couple of tentmakers, expelled from Rome with the other Jews. Paul lived and worked with them at Corinth. They “risked their lives” for him, he says, and “all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.”

circle.name: Gamaliel
circle.text: His teacher, a Pharisee “honored by all the people”. When the council wanted to kill the apostles, Gamaliel told them to leave them alone. If their work was from God, “you will not be able to stop them.”

circle.name: Stephen
circle.text: The first martyr, “full of grace and power”. Paul never forgot his death. Years later he told the Lord, “I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him.”

circle.name: Onesimus
circle.text: A slave of Paul's friend Philemon, who became a Christian through Paul in prison. Paul sent him back with a short letter, asking Philemon to take him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.”

death.big: He died at Rome under the emperor Nero. The early writers say he was beheaded, and buried by the road to Ostia.
paras: Acts ends with him still waiting for his trial in Rome, and does not tell how he died. Eusebius passes on what was said: that Paul made his defence, went out to preach again, and “upon coming to the same city a second time he suffered martyrdom.”

About 97, Clement of Rome wrote that Paul had been “seven times thrown into captivity, compelled to flee, and stoned.” He had “taught righteousness to the whole world, and come to the extreme limit of the west, and suffered martyrdom under the prefects.” Paul had hoped to reach Spain. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* thinks Clement's words make that journey probable.
Tertullian, about 200, wrote that at Rome “Paul wins his crown in a death like John's”, the death of John the Baptist, who was beheaded. Eusebius says plainly that “Paul was beheaded in Rome itself”.

Jerome says it was “in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter”, and that Paul “was buried in the Ostian way”. About 200, Gaius of Rome could already point visitors to the apostles' memorials on the Vatican Hill and the Ostian Way. The basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls stands over the grave.
John Chrysostom loved Rome for Paul's sake, and for Peter's. He pictured the two rising from their graves on the last day: “What a rose will Rome send up to Christ!”

later.title: Later stories
later.text: The *Acts of Paul*, a story written in the second century, says that when his head was struck off, “milk spurted upon the cloak of the soldier.” The Coptic Synaxarium tells how a young woman of Nero's family lent him her veil, and he wrapped his head in it. An old tradition puts the place at Aquae Salviae, today's Tre Fontane, about two miles from his grave.

kin.name: John Chrysostom
kin.text: He preached or wrote on every one of Paul's letters, and longed to see the dust of Paul's heart. A historian says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing.
